tf-variable-precedence.title: Resolve input variables by precedence
tf-variable-precedence.description:
One input variable can be given a value in several places at once. Terraform reads the places in a fixed
order and **the last one read wins**. Write `resolveVariables(declared, env, files, cli)` that reports the
final value of every declared variable and where it came from.

**Inputs**

- `declared`: dict from variable name to a dict that may contain `"default"`. (`{"default": None}` is a real
  default of null; `{}` means no default.)
- `env`: dict of environment variables. Only names of the exact form `TF_VAR_<name>` matter.
- `files`: dict from filename to a dict of `name → value`. These are the variable files in the working folder.
- `cli`: list of `[flag, argument]` pairs in the order typed: `["-var", "name=value"]` or
  `["-var-file", filename]` (the filename is always a key of `files`).

**Order of reading, lowest priority first**

1. the `default` in the declaration;
2. environment variables;
3. the file `terraform.tfvars`, if present;
4. the file `terraform.tfvars.json`, if present;
5. every file whose name ends in `.auto.tfvars` or `.auto.tfvars.json`, in alphabetical order of filename;
6. `-var` and `-var-file` options, in the order given.

Any other file in `files` is read **only** if a `-var-file` option names it.

For `-var`, the name is the text before the first `=` and the value is everything after it, as a string.
Values for names that are not declared are ignored in this exercise.

**Output.** A dict from each declared name to `[value, source]`, where `source` is `"default"`, `"env"`,
the filename, or `"-var"`. A variable that received no value at all maps to `[None, "missing"]`.

**Example:** declared `{"region": {"default": "ap-southeast-1"}, "size": {}}`, env `{"TF_VAR_size": "small"}`,
files `{"terraform.tfvars": {"size": "medium"}}`, cli `[]` →
`{"region": ["ap-southeast-1", "default"], "size": ["medium", "terraform.tfvars"]}`
tf-variable-precedence.starter:
def resolveVariables(declared, env, files, cli):
    pass

guide.prereqs: Setting variable values in *Variables, outputs, references and a configurable web server*. Python dicts, `str.startswith`, `str.partition`.
guide.intuition: Think of a whiteboard with one box per variable. Terraform walks through the sources from weakest to strongest and writes each value it finds into the box, wiping whatever was there. Whatever is on the board at the end is the answer. So the whole task is to visit the sources in the right order; no comparison logic is needed.
hints: Start by filling the result from the defaults, using `"default" in spec` (not `spec.get`) so that a null default is still a default.
Write one `assign(name, value, source)` helper that ignores undeclared names, and call it from every source in turn.
Three groups of files are read automatically: two fixed names, then the `.auto.` files sorted by name. Everything else waits for `-var-file`.
guide.brute_force: For each variable separately, search every source from strongest to weakest and stop at the first hit. It gives the same answers at O(variables × sources) cost, but the command-line options have to be scanned backwards, which is easy to get wrong. One forward pass that overwrites is shorter and mirrors what Terraform does.
guide.approach:
1. Defaults → `[default, "default"]`, or `[None, "missing"]`.
2. Environment: for each key starting with exactly `TF_VAR_`, assign the remainder of the key.
3. `terraform.tfvars`, then `terraform.tfvars.json`, when present.
4. `sorted(files)` filtered to names ending `.auto.tfvars` or `.auto.tfvars.json`.
5. Command line in order: `-var` → `partition("=")`; `-var-file` → load that file.

**Dry run:** `size` has default `micro`; env `TF_VAR_size=small`; `terraform.tfvars` says `medium`; `z.auto.tfvars` says `auto`; command line `-var size=first -var-file prod.tfvars` where the file says `file`.

| source read | box for `size` |
|---|---|
| default | micro |
| env | small |
| terraform.tfvars | medium |
| z.auto.tfvars | auto |
| -var | first |
| -var-file prod.tfvars | file |

Final: `["file", "prod.tfvars"]`. The `-var` did not win, because a later option on the same command line overrode it.
guide.complexity: Time O(V + E + F log F + A + C) for V variables, E environment entries, F files, A total assignments in loaded files and C options. Space O(V).
guide.pitfalls: Loading every `.tfvars` file in the folder (first wrong solution): `prod.tfvars` is never read unless named. Giving the environment priority over files (second wrong solution): environment variables are the *weakest* source after defaults, which surprises people who set `TF_VAR_x` and see no effect. Splitting `-var` on every `=` and losing part of the value, or treating a null default as missing (third wrong solution). Matching `tf_var_` in lower case.
guide.follow_up: Real Terraform is stricter about undeclared names: it ignores them in the environment, prints a warning for a variable file, and stops with an error for `-var`. Return a second list holding those warnings and errors.

tf-interpolate.title: Render a string template
tf-interpolate.description:
Inside a quoted string, `${ ... }` asks Terraform to evaluate a reference and insert the result. Write
`render(template, values)` for a simplified version of that.

- `values` maps a reference, written exactly as in code (`"var.name"`, `"local.env"`,
  `"aws_instance.web.id"`), to its value.
- Scan the template from left to right:
  - the three characters `$${` are an **escape**: they produce the two literal characters `${`, and nothing
    is looked up;
  - otherwise `${` starts an interpolation that ends at the next `}`. The text between, with surrounding
    spaces removed, is the reference to look up;
  - any other character is copied unchanged.
- Converting a value to text: a string is inserted as it is; a whole number in decimal; a bool as `true` or
  `false` in lower case.

Errors (return the message for the **first** problem met, scanning left to right):

- the reference is not a key of `values` → `"Error: undeclared reference <ref>"`;
- the value is `None`, a list or a dict → `"Error: invalid template value for <ref>"`.

Every unescaped `${` in the tests has a closing `}`.

**Example 1:** `render("web-${var.env}-${ var.index }", {"var.env": "prod", "var.index": 2})` → `"web-prod-2"`

**Example 2:** `render("echo $${HOME} on ${var.host}", {"var.host": "db1"})` → `"echo ${HOME} on db1"`

guide.prereqs: References and interpolation in *Variables, outputs, references and a configurable web server*. Walking a string with an index; `str.startswith(prefix, position)`.
guide.intuition: Read the template the way you would read a sentence aloud, one character at a time, with two special signals. `$${` means 'say a literal dollar-brace and carry on'. `${` means 'pause, look something up, say the answer, then resume after the closing brace'. Checking for the longer signal first is what stops the escape from being mistaken for an interpolation.
hints: Use a `while` loop with an index instead of a `for` loop, because you sometimes skip several characters at once.
Test for `$${` before testing for `${`. What would go wrong the other way round?
Python's `True` is also an `int`. Check `isinstance(value, bool)` before the general number case.
guide.brute_force: Call `str.replace` once per entry in `values` (first wrong solution). It handles the plain cases but cannot see escapes, spaces inside the braces, undeclared references, or a substituted value that itself looks like a template.
guide.approach:
Keep `i` and a list of output pieces.

- `template.startswith("$${", i)` → append `${`, `i += 3`.
- `template.startswith("${", i)` → `end = template.index("}", i)`; `ref = template[i+2:end].strip()`; look it up, convert, `i = end + 1`.
- otherwise copy one character.

**Dry run** on `echo $${HOME} on ${var.host}` with `var.host = "db1"`:

| i | sees | action | output so far |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0–4 | `echo ` | copy | `echo ` |
| 5 | `$${` | escape | `echo ${` |
| 8–12 | `HOME}` | copy | `echo ${HOME}` |
| 13–16 | ` on ` | copy | `echo ${HOME} on ` |
| 17 | `${` | look up `var.host` | `echo ${HOME} on db1` |

Each inserted value is appended to the output and never scanned again, so a value containing `${` stays literal.
guide.complexity: Time O(n) for a template of length n plus the length of inserted values; space O(n) for the output.
guide.pitfalls: Missing the escape (third wrong solution): shell scripts in `user_data` are full of `${HOME}`-style text that must reach the server untouched. Printing Python's `True` instead of `true` (second wrong solution). Re-scanning substituted text. A lone `$` or `%` is ordinary text. Reporting the second error instead of the first.
guide.follow_up: Terraform has a second template sequence, `%{ ... }`, for directives such as `%{ if }` and `%{ for }`, with `%%{` as its escape. Add the escape, then a simple `%{ if var.flag }...%{ endif }`.

tests.expected: Error: invalid template value for var.items
Error: invalid template value for var.nothing

tf-module-outputs.title: Wire module outputs to root outputs
tf-module-outputs.description:
Modules talk to each other only through inputs and outputs, and the root configuration does the wiring.
Write `resolveOutputs(root_vars, modules, outputs)` that follows the wires and computes the root outputs.

**Inputs**

- `root_vars`: dict of the root module's input variables, `name → value`.
- `modules`: dict from a module call's name to
  `{"inputs": {input_name: expression}, "outputs": {output_name: expression}}`.
  - `inputs` are the arguments written inside the `module` block. They are evaluated in the **root** scope.
  - `outputs` are the `output` blocks inside the module. They are evaluated in the **module's own** scope.
- `outputs`: dict of root outputs, `name → expression`, evaluated in the root scope.

**Expressions.** A string beginning with `var.` or `module.` is a reference. Any other value (a number, a
bool, a list, or a string without those prefixes) is a literal and evaluates to itself.

**Scopes**

- Root scope: `var.<name>` is a root variable; `module.<call>.<output>` is that module's output.
- Module scope: `var.<name>` is one of *that module's* inputs. Nothing else is visible: a module cannot see
  root variables or other modules, so any `module.` reference inside a module's outputs is undeclared.

**Undeclared references.** If following a root output's chain reaches a reference to something that does
not exist, that output's value is the string `"Error: undeclared <reference>"`, with the reference exactly
as written at the point of failure. Other outputs are unaffected. There are no circular references.

Return a dict from each root output name to its value.

**Example:** root variable `project = "shop"`; module `net` with input `name = var.project` and output
`vpc_name = var.name`; module `app` with input `network = module.net.vpc_name` and output
`summary = var.network`; root output `where = module.app.summary` → `{"where": "shop"}`

guide.prereqs: Module inputs and outputs in *Reusable modules: inputs, outputs and locals*; passing one module's output to another in *Worked project, part 2: database, container service, DNS and environments*. Recursion.
guide.intuition: A module is a sealed box with labelled sockets. Inside the box, `var.x` means 'whatever is plugged into my socket x'. Outside, `module.box.y` means 'whatever comes out of socket y'. Evaluating an output is following a cable: out of one box, into the root, perhaps into another box, until you reach a literal or a root variable. The one rule that must never be broken is that the meaning of `var.` depends on which side of the box wall you are standing.
hints: Write two evaluators, one for each scope, instead of one evaluator with flags. They call each other.
In root scope, `module.a.b` means: find module `a`'s output `b` and evaluate *that expression in module scope*.
In module scope, `var.x` means: find the argument `x` in the module call and evaluate *that expression in root scope*.
guide.brute_force: Repeatedly sweep over every expression, replacing references whose targets are already known, until nothing changes. It reaches the answer in at most as many sweeps as the longest chain, O(chain × expressions), and needs extra care for errors. Direct recursion follows only the chains the root outputs need.
guide.approach:
`eval_root(expr)`:
- literal → itself;
- `var.n` → `root_vars[n]`, or fail;
- `module.c.o` → must split into exactly three parts naming an existing call and output; then `eval_module(c, modules[c]["outputs"][o])`.

`eval_module(c, expr)`:
- literal → itself;
- `var.n` → `eval_root(modules[c]["inputs"][n])`, or fail if the call passes no such argument;
- `module.…` → fail: not visible here.

Failure is an exception carrying the reference text, caught once per root output.

**Dry run** of the example, output `where = module.app.summary`:

| step | scope | expression | goes to |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | root | module.app.summary | app's output `summary` |
| 2 | app | var.network | app's argument `network` |
| 3 | root | module.net.vpc_name | net's output `vpc_name` |
| 4 | net | var.name | net's argument `name` |
| 5 | root | var.project | `"shop"` |
guide.complexity: Time O(L) per root output for a chain of length L (O(R·L) in total without caching; add a memo dict to share work between outputs). Space O(L) for the recursion.
guide.pitfalls: Letting a module read root variables when it has no such input (first wrong solution): this is the scope leak that modules exist to prevent, and Terraform reports `Reference to undeclared input variable`. Resolving only one hop and returning the text `var.x` as if it were a value (second wrong solution). Accepting `module.net` or `module.net.e.x` as valid. Letting one broken output abort the others.
guide.follow_up: Give each module a `defaults` dict for inputs the caller may omit, and add `local.` references evaluated within their own scope.

tf-cidrsubnet.title: Implement cidrsubnet
tf-cidrsubnet.description:
Terraform's built-in `cidrsubnet(prefix, newbits, netnum)` carves a smaller network out of a larger one, so
that subnet ranges can be computed instead of typed. Implement it for IPv4.

- `prefix` is a network in CIDR notation, such as `"10.20.0.0/16"`: four numbers 0–255 and a prefix length
  0–32 saying how many leading bits are fixed.
- `newbits` (≥ 0) is how many extra bits to fix. The result's prefix length is the old length plus `newbits`.
- `netnum` chooses which of the `2 ** newbits` possible subnets to return, counting from 0. Its binary digits
  are written into the newly fixed bit positions.

If `prefix` has any bits set after its prefix length (for example `"10.20.5.7/16"`), clear them first.

Errors, checked in this order:

1. the new prefix length would exceed 32 → `"Error: insufficient address space"`;
2. `netnum` is negative or does not fit in `newbits` bits → `"Error: netnum out of range"`.

Return the subnet in CIDR notation.

**Example 1:** `cidrsubnet("10.20.0.0/16", 8, 11)` → `"10.20.11.0/24"`

**Example 2:** `cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/24", 2, 3)` → `"10.0.0.192/26"`
tf-cidrsubnet.solution:
def cidrsubnet(prefix, newbits, netnum):
    ip, length = prefix.split("/")
    length = int(length)
    new_length = length + newbits
    if new_length > 32:
        return "Error: insufficient address space"
    if netnum < 0 or netnum >= 2 ** newbits:
        return "Error: netnum out of range"
    a, b, c, d = (int(part) for part in ip.split("."))
    address = (a << 24) | (b << 16) | (c << 8) | d
    mask = ((1 << length) - 1) << (32 - length)
    address &= mask
    address |= netnum << (32 - new_length)
    octets = [(address >> shift) & 255 for shift in (24, 16, 8, 0)]
    return ".".join(str(o) for o in octets) + "/" + str(new_length)

guide.prereqs: `cidrsubnet` in *Worked project, part 1: repository, remote state, network and security groups*. CIDR notation; binary numbers and the bit operators `<<`, `>>`, `&`, `|`.
guide.intuition: An IPv4 address is one 32-bit number written as four bytes. A prefix length of 16 says the first 16 bits are the network's name and the remaining 16 are free. `cidrsubnet` extends the name by `newbits` bits and writes `netnum` into exactly those new positions. Converted to a single integer, that is one shift and one OR; the dotted form is only how the number is printed.
hints: Combine the four numbers into one integer: `a << 24 | b << 16 | c << 8 | d`.
The new bits sit immediately after the old prefix. Their lowest bit is `32 - new_length` positions from the right, so shift `netnum` left by that amount.
To print, extract each byte with a shift and `& 255`.
guide.brute_force: List every subnet of the new size inside the network in order and return the one at position `netnum`. Correct, but O(2^newbits) time; `newbits` of 14 already means 16,384 steps for one answer. The bit arithmetic is O(1).
guide.approach:
1. Split into address and length; `new_length = length + newbits`.
2. Validate: `new_length > 32`, then `netnum` outside `0 .. 2**newbits - 1`.
3. Pack the four bytes into one integer.
4. Clear host bits with a mask of `length` ones followed by zeros: `((1 << length) - 1) << (32 - length)`.
5. `address |= netnum << (32 - new_length)`.
6. Unpack into four bytes and append `/new_length`.

**Dry run:** `cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/24", 2, 3)`.

- `new_length = 26`. `netnum = 3` fits in 2 bits (0–3).
- The last byte in binary is `00 000000`: two new network bits, then six host bits.
- `3 << (32 - 26)` = `3 << 6` = 192 = `11 000000`.
- Result `10.0.0.192/26`.

For the lesson's network: `/16` plus 8 bits puts `netnum` in the third byte, so 11 gives `10.20.11.0/24`.
guide.complexity: Time O(1) and space O(1): a fixed number of arithmetic operations on 32-bit values.
guide.pitfalls: Adding `netnum` to one of the dotted numbers (first wrong solution): it happens to work when the new bits fill exactly one byte and breaks when they straddle bytes or stop mid-byte, as in `/12 + 4` or `/24 + 2`. Skipping validation or leaving host bits in place (second wrong solution), which yields nonsense such as overlapping subnets. Checking `netnum > 2 ** newbits` instead of `>=`. Writing `1 << length - 1` and expecting `(1 << length) - 1`: subtraction binds tighter than a shift, so add the parentheses.
guide.follow_up: Implement `cidrhost(prefix, hostnum)`, which returns one address inside a network, and `cidrsubnets(prefix, newbits...)`, which allocates several consecutive subnets of different sizes.

tf-dependency-order.title: Build the dependency graph and an apply order
tf-dependency-order.description:
Terraform finds dependencies by spotting references to other resources inside a resource's arguments, then
creates resources so that everything a resource refers to already exists. Write `applyOrder(config)`.

`config` maps each resource address (always of the form `type.name`, lower-case letters, digits and
underscores) to a list of expression strings taken from its arguments, for example
`{"aws_instance.web": ["aws_subnet.public.id", "[aws_security_group.web.id]"]}`.

**Finding references.** Resource `A` depends on resource `B` (with `B != A`) when `B`'s address occurs in one
of `A`'s expressions as a whole reference: the character immediately before the occurrence must not be a
letter, digit, underscore or dot, and the character immediately after must not be a letter, digit or underscore.
(So `aws_vpc.main` is referenced by `aws_vpc.main.id` and by `[aws_vpc.main.id]`, but not by
`aws_vpc.main2.id`, `my_aws_vpc.main.id` or `module.net.aws_vpc.main.id`.) Text that names something not in
`config` is ignored.

**Ordering.** Repeatedly pick, among the resources whose dependencies have all been picked already, the one
with the alphabetically smallest address. The input is guaranteed to contain no cycles.

Return the list of addresses in that order.

**Example:** `{"aws_subnet.a": ["aws_vpc.main.id"], "aws_vpc.main": ["10.0.0.0/16"], "aws_eip.x": []}`
→ `["aws_eip.x", "aws_vpc.main", "aws_subnet.a"]`

guide.prereqs: References and the dependency graph in *Variables, outputs, references and a configurable web server*. Topological sorting; a min-heap (`heapq`).
guide.intuition: Two separate jobs. First turn text into edges by recognising whole references. Then produce a topological order, and make it deterministic by always choosing the smallest address that is ready: Kahn's algorithm with a priority queue instead of a plain queue.
hints: A plain substring test is not enough: `aws_vpc.main` occurs inside `aws_vpc.main2`. Check the characters on both sides of each occurrence.
Count, for every resource, how many dependencies are not yet created. Those with zero are ready.
Keep the ready set in a min-heap. Pop the smallest, then decrement the counts of its dependents and push any that reach zero.
guide.brute_force: Recompute the full ready set and sort it after every pick: O(V) picks, each O(V log V) plus set comparisons, about O(V² log V). Correct, and fine for small inputs. The heap version is O((V + E) log V) after edge discovery.
guide.approach:
**Edges.** For each pair (A, B) with A ≠ B, scan A's expressions for occurrences of B's address and accept an occurrence when the previous character is not an identifier character or a dot and the next is not an identifier character. A dot *after* is fine (`.id`); so is `[`.

**Order.** `remaining[A]` = number of dependencies. Heap = all with zero. Pop the smallest, append it, and release its dependents.

**Dry run:** `a.first` needs `z.last`; `b.mid` needs `a.first`; `c.free` and `z.last` need nothing.

| heap before | pop | released |
|---|---|---|
| c.free, z.last | c.free | — |
| z.last | z.last | a.first |
| a.first | a.first | b.mid |
| b.mid | b.mid | — |

Result `["c.free", "z.last", "a.first", "b.mid"]`. Note `a.first` could not jump ahead of `c.free` merely because it sorts first: it was not ready.
guide.complexity: Edge discovery is O(V² · L) for V resources and total expression length L in this simple form. The ordering is O((V + E) log V). Space O(V + E).
guide.pitfalls: Substring matching without boundaries. Counting a self-reference as a dependency. Emitting whole 'waves' in sorted order (the third wrong solution): that differs from smallest-ready-first when a newly released resource sorts before something still waiting in the same wave. Returning plain alphabetical order.
guide.follow_up: Group the result into waves of resources that can be created in parallel, as `terraform apply` does with its default parallelism of 10.

tf-destroy-order.title: Compute a destroy order
tf-destroy-order.description:
Destroying happens in the reverse of creation order: anything that depends on a resource must go first.
Write `destroyOrder(depends_on, targets)`.

- `depends_on` maps every resource address to the list of addresses it depends on (all of them keys; no cycles).
- `targets` is a list of addresses someone asked to destroy.

**What gets destroyed.** The set `S` of every target plus every resource that depends on a member of `S`,
directly or through a chain. (You cannot leave a subnet behind when its VPC is deleted.)

**In which order.** First compute the *creation* order of `S` alone: repeatedly pick, among the members of `S`
whose dependencies inside `S` have all been picked, the alphabetically smallest. Dependencies outside `S` are
ignored. The destroy order is that list reversed.

Return the destroy order.

**Example:** `{"vpc": [], "subnet": ["vpc"], "db": ["subnet"], "app": ["subnet", "db"], "dns": []}` with
`targets = ["subnet"]` → creation order of `{subnet, db, app}` is `subnet, db, app`, so the answer is
`["app", "db", "subnet"]`. The VPC and the DNS record are untouched.

guide.prereqs: Creation and destruction order in *Variables, outputs, references and a configurable web server*. The problem *Build the dependency graph and an apply order*.
guide.intuition: Destroying one thing drags along everything built on top of it. So: find the doomed set by walking *up* the graph from the targets, then order that set exactly as you would for creation and flip the list.
hints: Reverse the edges to get, for each resource, the list of resources that depend on it.
Flood-fill from the targets along those reversed edges to collect the doomed set.
Run the smallest-ready-first topological sort on the doomed set only, ignoring edges that leave the set, then reverse.
guide.brute_force: Compute the creation order of the whole system, reverse it, and filter to the doomed set. That is simpler but is *not* the same definition: restricting to the set first can change which resource is 'smallest ready' at each step. Follow the stated definition.
guide.approach:
1. Build `dependents`.
2. Depth-first search from each target over `dependents` → `doomed`.
3. `remaining[a]` = number of distinct dependencies of `a` inside `doomed`.
4. Min-heap Kahn's algorithm over `doomed` → creation order; reverse it.

**Dry run** with targets `["subnet"]`: doomed = `{subnet, db, app}`.

| step | ready heap | pick |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | subnet (its only dependency, vpc, is outside the set) | subnet |
| 2 | db | db |
| 3 | app | app |

Creation `[subnet, db, app]`, destroy `[app, db, subnet]`.
guide.complexity: Time O((V + E) log V); space O(V + E).
guide.pitfalls: Destroying only the listed targets and leaving dependents pointing at nothing. Sorting the doomed set alphabetically and reversing, which ignores dependencies. Counting a duplicated dependency twice so a counter never reaches zero. Duplicate targets.
guide.follow_up: `terraform destroy -target=X` behaves this way and prints a warning. Explain why routine use of `-target` is discouraged.

tf-cycle-detect.title: Detect a dependency cycle with a helpful message
tf-cycle-detect.description:
If resources depend on each other in a loop, nothing can be created first and Terraform stops with
`Error: Cycle`. A good error names the loop. Write `findCycle(depends_on)`.

`depends_on` maps each resource address to the list of addresses it depends on. Entries that are not keys of
`depends_on` are ignored. A resource may list itself.

- If there is no cycle, return the empty string `""`.
- Otherwise return `"Cycle: n1 -> n2 -> ... -> n1"` where `a -> b` means "a depends on b", chosen as follows
  so that the answer is unique:
  1. Let `s` be the alphabetically smallest address that lies on at least one cycle.
  2. Among all cycles that start and end at `s`, take the shortest (fewest arrows).
  3. If several are equally short, take the one whose sequence of addresses is alphabetically smallest
     (compare the second address, then the third, and so on).

**Example 1:** `{"a": ["b"], "b": ["c"], "c": ["a"]}` → `"Cycle: a -> b -> c -> a"`

**Example 2:** `{"web": ["sg"], "sg": ["web"], "db": []}` → `"Cycle: sg -> web -> sg"`

**Example 3:** `{"a": ["a"]}` → `"Cycle: a -> a"`

guide.prereqs: The dependency graph and `Error: Cycle` in *Variables, outputs, references and a configurable web server*. Breadth-first search for shortest paths.
guide.intuition: 'Is there a cycle?' is easy; 'which one, reproducibly?' needs a rule. A cycle through `s` is a path that leaves `s` and comes back. If you know, for every node, how many arrows it takes to get back to `s`, you can walk from `s` choosing at each step the smallest neighbour that is exactly one arrow closer to home. That walk is the shortest cycle and, among the shortest, the alphabetically smallest.
hints: Try each address in alphabetical order as the candidate `s`; the first one that lies on a cycle is the answer's start.
Run a breadth-first search *backwards* from `s` (over reversed edges) to get `dist[x]` = arrows needed from `x` to `s`.
`s` is on a cycle when one of its own dependencies has a distance. Then greedily step to the smallest neighbour with distance one less.
guide.brute_force: Enumerate every simple path starting at each node with depth-first search and keep the best cycle found. Exponential in the worst case. The breadth-first approach is polynomial.
guide.approach:
For `s` in sorted order:

1. Reverse BFS from `s` gives `dist`.
2. Candidates = dependencies of `s` that have a distance. None → `s` is on no cycle; try the next address.
3. `best` = smallest candidate distance. First step = smallest candidate with that distance.
4. From there, repeatedly move to the smallest dependency whose distance is exactly one less, until reaching `s`.

**Dry run** on `{"a": ["b"], "b": ["c", "d"], "c": ["e"], "d": ["e"], "e": ["a"]}` with `s = a`:
distances to `a`: e = 1, c = 2, d = 2, b = 3. Start at `a`; its only dependency `b` has distance 3. From `b`, both `c` and `d` have distance 2; pick `c`. Then `e` (1), then `a` (0).
Answer: `Cycle: a -> b -> c -> e -> a`.

Why a plain depth-first search fails (second wrong solution): on `{"a": ["b", "c"], "b": ["d"], "c": ["a"], "d": ["a"]}` it explores `b` first and reports `a -> b -> d -> a`, missing the shorter `a -> c -> a`.
guide.complexity: One reverse BFS is O(V + E); at most V candidates → O(V·(V + E)) time, O(V + E) space. The neighbour lists are sorted once.
guide.pitfalls: Detecting only self-loops and two-node loops. Reporting whichever cycle depth-first search meets first, which is neither shortest nor deterministic by the stated rule. Starting from a node that leads *into* a cycle without being on it (`a` in `{"z": ["y"], "y": ["z"], "a": ["z"]}`). Following dependencies on addresses that are not declared.
guide.follow_up: Real cycles often come from security groups that reference each other inline. Explain how separate rule resources break such a cycle.

tests.expected: Cycle: a -> b -> c -> e -> a

tf-create-before-destroy.title: Order the steps of a replacement plan
tf-create-before-destroy.description:
Several resources are all being **replaced** in one apply. Some have `create_before_destroy = true`. Work out
the order of operations. Write `replacementSteps(resources)`.

`resources` is a list of dicts `{"address": str, "cbd": bool, "depends_on": [addresses]}`. Every resource in
the list is being replaced; `depends_on` only mentions addresses in the list; there are no cycles.

**Rule 1: propagation.** If a resource has `create_before_destroy`, every resource it depends on, directly or
through a chain, is treated as having it too. (Otherwise the old dependency would be destroyed while the old
dependent still needs it.) Call the result the *effective* setting.

**Rule 2: three phases.**

1. **Destroy first.** Every resource whose effective setting is false is destroyed now, dependents before
   their dependencies. Step text: `"destroy <address>"`.
2. **Create.** Every resource is created, dependencies before dependents. Step text: `"create <address>"`.
3. **Destroy deposed.** Every resource whose effective setting is true has its old object destroyed,
   dependents before their dependencies. Step text: `"destroy deposed <address>"`.

**Tie-breaking.** "Dependencies before dependents" means: repeatedly pick the alphabetically smallest address
whose dependencies (within the group being ordered) are all picked. "Dependents before dependencies" is that
same order reversed. In phases 1 and 3 the ordering is computed over only the resources in that phase.

Return the list of step strings.

**Example:** `lt` (cbd true, no dependencies) and `asg` (cbd false, depends on `lt`) →
`["destroy asg", "create lt", "create asg", "destroy deposed lt"]`

guide.prereqs: `create_before_destroy` and its spread to dependencies in *Zero-downtime deployment, plans that fail and safe refactoring*. The apply-order problem in this track.
guide.intuition: Replacement order is decided per resource, but resources are linked. If the new server must exist before the old one is removed, then the old firewall it uses must also survive until then, so the setting flows *down* to dependencies. After that, the apply is three sweeps: tear down what may go first, build everything, sweep away the kept-alive old objects.
hints: Compute the effective setting first: start from every resource with the flag and walk its dependencies, marking each one.
Write one helper that returns the smallest-ready-first creation order for any subset of resources.
Phase 1 is the reversed order of the non-flagged subset, phase 2 the order of everything, phase 3 the reversed order of the flagged subset.
guide.brute_force: Handle each resource independently in alphabetical order, as the second wrong solution does. It ignores dependencies entirely and produces orders such as creating a server before its launch template.
guide.approach:
**Propagate.** Stack = flagged resources. Pop one, mark each unmarked dependency as flagged and push it.

**Order.** `creation_order(group)`: Kahn's algorithm with a min-heap, counting only dependencies inside the group.

**Dry run:** `net`, `sg → net`, `lt (cbd) → sg`, `asg → lt, net`, `dns`.

- Propagation: `lt` flags `sg`, which flags `net`. Effective true: `{lt, sg, net}`; false: `{asg, dns}`.
- Phase 1 (false group, creation order `asg, dns`, reversed): `destroy dns`, `destroy asg`.
- Phase 2 (all): `create dns`, `create net`, `create sg`, `create lt`, `create asg`.
- Phase 3 (true group, creation order `net, sg, lt`, reversed): `destroy deposed lt`, `destroy deposed sg`, `destroy deposed net`.
guide.complexity: Time O((V + E) log V) for three topological sorts; space O(V + E).
guide.pitfalls: Skipping propagation (first wrong solution): the old dependency is destroyed in phase 1 while the old dependent still exists. Propagating in the wrong direction, to dependents. Ordering phase 1 and phase 3 by the full graph instead of within their own group. Duplicate entries in `depends_on`.
guide.follow_up: Why does `create_before_destroy` require unique names? Add a `fixed_name` flag and report a name-collision error for flagged resources that have it.

tf-count-plan.title: Plan a count resource after its list changes
tf-count-plan.description:
A resource written with `count` is a numbered row of copies: `aws_iam_user.staff[0]`, `aws_iam_user.staff[1]`
and so on. Terraform identifies each copy **by its position**, not by what it contains. Write
`countPlan(resource, old_values, new_values, force_new)` to show what that does to a plan.

- `resource` is the address without an index, for example `"aws_iam_user.staff"`.
- `old_values[i]` is the value copy `i` was created with (what state remembers).
- `new_values[i]` is the value the configuration now gives copy `i`.
- `force_new` is `True` when the value cannot be changed in place (a user's name, for instance).

For every index from `0` up to the longer list's last index, decide one action:

| Situation at index `i` | Action |
|---|---|
| Only in `new_values` | `"create"` |
| Only in `old_values` | `"delete"` |
| In both, values equal | `"no-op"` |
| In both, values differ, `force_new` is true | `"replace"` |
| In both, values differ, `force_new` is false | `"update"` |

Return a list of `[address, action]` pairs in index order, where the address is `resource[i]`.

**Example:** `countPlan("aws_iam_user.staff", ["asha", "ben", "chidi"], ["asha", "chidi"], True)` →
`[["aws_iam_user.staff[0]", "no-op"], ["aws_iam_user.staff[1]", "replace"], ["aws_iam_user.staff[2]", "delete"]]`

Ben was removed from the middle, yet the plan replaces index 1 (Ben becomes Chidi) and deletes index 2
(the original Chidi). That is the index-shifting trap.
tf-count-plan.starter:
def countPlan(resource, old_values, new_values, force_new):
    pass

guide.prereqs: The lesson *Loops: count, for_each and the index-shifting trap*. Python lists and `range`.
guide.intuition: With `count`, the address *is* the position. Terraform never asks 'where did Ben go?'. It asks 'what is at index 1 now, and what was there before?'. So compare the two lists slot by slot, like two columns of a spreadsheet, and ignore the fact that the same value may appear in a different row.
hints: Loop over indices, not over values. How many indices are there in total?
An index past the end of the old list is new; an index past the end of the new list is going away.
For an index in both lists, compare the two values at that index only. `force_new` chooses between replace and update.
guide.brute_force: There is no slower natural approach: one pass over the indices is already the direct translation of the rule. The tempting *wrong* approach is a set difference between the two lists, which describes `for_each`, not `count`.
guide.approach:
1. `n = max(len(old_values), len(new_values))`.
2. For each `i` in `range(n)`: past the old list → `create`; past the new list → `delete`; equal → `no-op`; otherwise `replace` or `update` depending on `force_new`.
3. Build the address with an f-string: `f"{resource}[{i}]"`.

**Dry run:** old `["asha", "ben", "chidi"]`, new `["asha", "chidi"]`, `force_new = True`.

| i | old | new | action |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | asha | asha | no-op |
| 1 | ben | chidi | replace |
| 2 | chidi | (none) | delete |

One person was removed, but the plan destroys two users and creates one. In the summary line that reads `1 to add, 0 to change, 2 to destroy`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n) for n = the longer list; space O(n) for the result.
guide.pitfalls: Matching by value instead of by position (first wrong solution): that reports a tidy single delete, which is exactly what Terraform does *not* do. Ignoring `force_new` and always reporting `update`. Stopping at the shorter list's length and losing the creates or deletes at the tail.
guide.follow_up: Removing the *last* element is the one harmless removal. Explain why, then solve *Plan a for_each resource after its keys change* and compare the two plans for the same removal.

tf-foreach-plan.title: Plan a for_each resource after its keys change
tf-foreach-plan.description:
A resource written with `for_each` has one copy per **key**: `aws_iam_user.staff["asha"]`,
`aws_iam_user.staff["ben"]`. The key is the identity, so removing one key touches only that copy.
Write `forEachPlan(resource, old, new, force_new)`.

`old` (what state holds) and `new` (what the configuration now says) are each **either**

- a dict, standing for a map: each key maps to the value that copy is built from; **or**
- a list of strings, standing for `toset([...])`: every distinct string is a key whose value is the
  string itself. Duplicates collapse into one key, and order means nothing.

For every key in either collection decide one action:

| Situation | Action |
|---|---|
| Key only in `new` | `"create"` |
| Key only in `old` | `"delete"` |
| In both, values equal | `"no-op"` |
| In both, values differ, `force_new` true | `"replace"` |
| In both, values differ, `force_new` false | `"update"` |

Return `[address, action]` pairs sorted by key, where the address is `resource["key"]` with the key in
double quotes.

**Example:** `forEachPlan("aws_iam_user.staff", ["asha", "ben", "chidi"], ["asha", "chidi"], True)` →
`[['aws_iam_user.staff["asha"]', "no-op"], ['aws_iam_user.staff["ben"]', "delete"], ['aws_iam_user.staff["chidi"]', "no-op"]]`
tf-foreach-plan.starter:
def forEachPlan(resource, old, new, force_new):
    pass

guide.prereqs: The lesson *Loops: count, for_each and the index-shifting trap*, and the problem *Plan a count resource after its list changes*. Python dicts and sets.
guide.intuition: With `for_each` the address carries a name tag instead of a seat number. Names do not shift when someone leaves the row. So the plan is a comparison of two dictionaries by key: which keys appeared, which vanished, and which kept their key but changed their value.
hints: Turn both inputs into dicts first. A list of strings becomes `{s: s for s in items}`, which also removes duplicates.
Walk the sorted union of the two key sets.
Only a key present on both sides can be a no-op, an update or a replacement. Compare the two values for that key.
guide.brute_force: For each key in `new`, scan `old` linearly to find a match, and the reverse for deletions: O(n·m). Dict lookups make each check O(1).
guide.approach:
1. Normalise: dict stays a dict; a list becomes a dict from each string to itself.
2. `keys = sorted(set(before) | set(after))`.
3. Decide per key with the table from the statement.
4. Address: `f'{resource}["{key}"]'`. Single quotes around the f-string let you write the double quotes directly.

**Dry run** with the same removal as the count problem: old `["asha", "ben", "chidi"]`, new `["asha", "chidi"]`.

| key | in old | in new | action |
|---|---|---|---|
| asha | yes | yes | no-op |
| ben | yes | no | delete |
| chidi | yes | yes | no-op |

One person removed, one resource destroyed. Compare with the count version of the same change: one replacement and one delete.
guide.complexity: Time O(k log k) for k distinct keys because of the sort; space O(k).
guide.pitfalls: Comparing by sorted position (first wrong solution), which reintroduces the index-shifting behaviour of `count`. Forgetting that a map's value can change while its key stays (second wrong solution). Forgetting to collapse duplicates in a list. Writing the address with single quotes or no quotes around the key.
guide.follow_up: Terraform rejects a plain list for `for_each` and asks for `toset(...)` or a map. Explain why a positional collection would defeat the purpose of `for_each`.

tf-for-expression.title: Evaluate a for expression
tf-for-expression.description:
A `for` expression walks a collection and builds a new list or map, optionally filtering as it goes.
Write `evalFor(collection, spec)` that evaluates one.

**Iteration.** `collection` is a list or a dict.

- A list is visited in order; the *key* is the index (0, 1, 2, …) and the *value* is the element.
- A dict stands for a map and is visited **in sorted key order**, whatever order it was written in.

**The spec** is a dict:

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `"out"` | `"list"` for `[for ... : value]`, `"map"` for `{for ... : key => value}` |
| `"value"` | a pair `[func, field]` producing each result value |
| `"key"` | a pair `[func, field]` producing each result key (map output only) |
| `"if"` | optional `[field, op, operand]` filter; items failing it are skipped |
| `"group"` | optional bool, map output only: the `...` grouping mode |

`field` is `"key"` or `"value"`. `func` is one of `"id"` (unchanged), `"upper"`, `"lower"`, `"length"`
(number of characters). `op` is one of `"=="`, `"!="`, `">"`, `"<"`.

**Results.**

- List output: the produced values, in iteration order.
- Map output: a dict. Result keys are always strings, so convert a numeric key with `str`.
  If two items produce the same key and `group` is not true, stop and return the string
  `Error: Duplicate object key "<key>"` for the first repeated key met.
  With `group` true, each key maps to the list of its values in iteration order.

**Example 1:** `evalFor(["web", "api"], {"out": "list", "value": ["upper", "value"]})` → `["WEB", "API"]`

**Example 2:** `evalFor({"ben": "web", "asha": "web", "chidi": "data"}, {"out": "map", "key": ["id", "value"], "value": ["id", "key"], "group": True})`
→ `{"web": ["asha", "ben"], "data": ["chidi"]}`

guide.prereqs: The lesson *For expressions, string directives and conditionals*. Python list and dict building, `sorted`, `dict.setdefault`.
guide.intuition: Every `for` expression is the same three-step machine: visit items in a fixed order, drop the ones the `if` rejects, and emit something for each survivor. The brackets decide the container. Two details make it Terraform rather than Python: maps are visited in sorted key order, and a map result may not receive the same key twice unless you asked for grouping.
hints: First build one list of `(key, value)` pairs: `enumerate` for a list, sorted items for a dict. Everything after that is the same for both.
Write two small helpers: one applies a `[func, field]` pair to an item, one tests the optional filter.
For map output keep a result dict. Before inserting, check whether the key is already there; what you do next depends on `group`.
guide.brute_force: Handle the four combinations (list or map input, list or map output) with four separate loops. It works and costs the same, but every rule is written four times and the sorted-order rule is easy to forget in one of them.
guide.approach:
1. `items` = `enumerate(collection)` for a list, `sorted(collection.items())` for a dict.
2. `produce([func, field], k, v)` picks `k` or `v` and applies the function.
3. `keep(k, v)` evaluates the filter, or returns `True` when there is none.
4. List output: a comprehension over `items`.
5. Map output: for each kept item compute `key = str(...)` and `value`. Grouping → `setdefault(key, []).append(value)`. No grouping and key already present → return the error string. Otherwise store it.

**Dry run** for `{for person, team in {"ben": "web", "asha": "web", "chidi": "data"} : team => person...}`:

| visited (sorted) | key | result so far |
|---|---|---|
| asha → web | web | `{web: [asha]}` |
| ben → web | web | `{web: [asha, ben]}` |
| chidi → data | data | `{web: [asha, ben], data: [chidi]}` |

Without the `...`, the second row meets `web` again and the answer is `Error: Duplicate object key "web"`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n log n) for a dict input because of the sort, O(n) for a list. Space O(n) for the result.
guide.pitfalls: Visiting a dict in the order it was written (first wrong solution): Terraform maps have no insertion order, so results would differ from the real tool. Letting a later item silently overwrite an earlier one with the same key (second wrong solution): Terraform refuses, because losing data without a word is worse than an error. Forgetting to convert a numeric key to a string. Applying the filter after checking for duplicates instead of before.
guide.follow_up: Add a `"set"` input kind (a list to be treated as a set of strings: de-duplicated and visited in sorted order), which is how `for_each = toset(...)` iterates.

tf-moved-blocks.title: Apply moved blocks to state addresses
tf-moved-blocks.description:
A `moved` block tells Terraform that an object has a new address, so a rename is recorded in state
instead of being planned as "destroy the old one, create a new one". Write `applyMoves(addresses, moves)`.

- `addresses` is the list of resource instance addresses currently in state, such as
  `aws_instance.web`, `aws_instance.web[0]`, `aws_iam_user.staff["asha"]` or `module.net.aws_vpc.main`.
- `moves` is a list of `[from, to]` pairs, applied **one after another in the order given**.

**What one move does.** An address `A` is affected by `[from, to]` when

- `A` equals `from`, or
- `A` starts with `from` immediately followed by `[` (an instance of that resource or module), or
- `A` starts with `from` immediately followed by `.` (something inside that module).

An affected address has its leading `from` replaced by `to`; the rest of the address is kept.
A move that affects nothing is skipped without complaint.

**Collisions.** If a rewritten address is the same as an address that this move does not affect, stop and
return a one-element list `["Error: <address> already exists"]`, using the alphabetically smallest such address.

Return the final addresses sorted alphabetically.

**Example:** `applyMoves(["aws_instance.web[0]", "aws_instance.web[1]", "aws_vpc.main"], [["aws_instance.web", "aws_instance.app"]])`
→ `["aws_instance.app[0]", "aws_instance.app[1]", "aws_vpc.main"]`

guide.prereqs: `moved` blocks in *State surgery: moving, removing, importing and repairing* and *Zero-downtime deployment, plans that fail and safe refactoring*. Resource addresses with indices and module prefixes. Python sets and `str.startswith`.
guide.intuition: State is a lookup table from address to real object. A move edits the left-hand column and never touches the objects. Because addresses nest (a module contains resources, a resource contains instances), renaming something higher up renames everything beneath it, the way renaming a folder changes the path of every file inside.
hints: A plain `startswith(from)` is too generous: `aws_instance.web` is a prefix of `aws_instance.web2`. Which character must come next for it to be the same resource?
Process one move at a time against the *current* set, so a later move can pick up what an earlier one produced.
Split the current set into addresses the move rewrites and addresses it leaves alone. A collision is a rewritten address that already sits in the second group.
guide.brute_force: For each move, loop over a list of addresses and rewrite matches in place, then scan the whole list for duplicates: O(m·n²) with the duplicate scan. Sets bring the collision check down to O(1) per address.
guide.approach:
For each `[from, to]`:

1. `rewritten = {A: to + A[len(from):]}` for every `A` that equals `from` or continues with `[` or `.`.
2. `staying = current - rewritten.keys()`.
3. Any rewritten address found in `staying` is a collision → return the error for the smallest one.
4. `current = staying ∪ rewritten.values()`.

**Dry run:** state `module.net.aws_vpc.main`, `module.net.aws_subnet.a[0]`, `module.network.aws_vpc.main`; move `module.net → module.core`.

| address | next character after `module.net` | affected | becomes |
|---|---|---|---|
| module.net.aws_vpc.main | `.` | yes | module.core.aws_vpc.main |
| module.net.aws_subnet.a[0] | `.` | yes | module.core.aws_subnet.a[0] |
| module.network.aws_vpc.main | `w` | no | unchanged |

The swap test (`a → tmp`, `b → a`, `tmp → b`) shows why moves must be applied in order: each step sees the result of the one before.
guide.complexity: Time O(m·n·L) for m moves, n addresses and address length L. Space O(n·L).
guide.pitfalls: Prefix matching without a boundary (first wrong solution) drags along unrelated resources whose names begin the same way, and `web[1]` would capture `web[10]`. Handling only exact matches (second wrong solution) misses every instance of a renamed `count` or `for_each` resource. Skipping the collision check (third wrong solution) merges two different real objects into one address, which in real life would orphan one of them.
guide.follow_up: Generate the `moved` blocks needed to convert a `count` resource to `for_each`: given the list of names, emit one `[resource[i], resource["name"]]` pair per index.

tf-parse-address.title: Parse a resource address
tf-parse-address.description:
Every object Terraform manages has an address, and plans, state commands and error messages all speak in
addresses. Write `parseAddress(address)` to take one apart.

An address is, from left to right:

1. zero or more module steps, each written `module.<name>` and optionally followed by an instance key;
2. optionally the word `data.` (a data source, which reads something, instead of a managed resource);
3. `<type>.<name>`, optionally followed by an instance key.

An **instance key** is `[<whole number>]` (from `count`) or `["<text>"]` (from `for_each`). The text between
the double quotes may contain any characters except a double quote, **including dots and square brackets**.
Module names, types and resource names contain only letters, digits, underscores and hyphens.

Return a dict:

```
{"modules": [[name, key], ...], "mode": "managed" or "data", "type": str, "name": str, "key": key}
```

where a key is `None` when absent, an `int` for a number and a `str` for quoted text.

**Example 1:** `"aws_instance.web[2]"` →
`{"modules": [], "mode": "managed", "type": "aws_instance", "name": "web", "key": 2}`

**Example 2:** `'module.net.module.subnets["app-a"].data.aws_ami.ubuntu'` →
`{"modules": [["net", None], ["subnets", "app-a"]], "mode": "data", "type": "aws_ami", "name": "ubuntu", "key": None}`

guide.prereqs: Resource addresses from *Installing Terraform, signing in safely and creating a first resource*, module addresses from *Reusable modules: inputs, outputs and locals*, and instance keys from *Loops: count, for_each and the index-shifting trap*. Scanning a string with an index.
guide.intuition: An address is a path, like a file path with dots for slashes. The catch is that a `for_each` key is free text and may itself contain dots, so you cannot split on dots blindly. Read the string left to right: take a name, then check whether a bracket follows, and if it opens with a quote, jump straight to the closing quote without inspecting what lies between.
hints: Tokenise first, interpret second. Produce a flat list of `[name, key]` steps before thinking about modules.
After a name, the next character is a dot, a `[`, or the end. For `["`, find the next double quote; for `[` and a digit, find the next `]`.
Then consume steps from the left: while the step is `module`, the following step is a module name. After the modules, an optional `data` step, and the last two steps are type and name.
guide.brute_force: Split on `.` and repair the pieces that were cut inside quotes by gluing them back together. It can be made to work, but the repair logic is harder to get right than a single left-to-right scan.
guide.approach:
**Tokenise.** Keep an index `i`. Advance `j` to the next `.` or `[`. The slice is a name. If `[` follows: a quote means a string key ending at the next quote; otherwise an integer ending at `]`. Skip the dot and repeat.

**Interpret.** With steps `parts` and a cursor `k`:

1. While `parts[k]` is named `module` *and more than two steps remain*, record `parts[k+1]` as a module step and move `k` on by two.
2. If `parts[k]` is named `data` and more than two steps remain, the mode is `data`; move on by one.
3. `parts[k]` is the type; `parts[k+1]` carries the name and the resource's key.

The "more than two steps remain" guard covers odd but legal names: a resource can be *named* `module` or `data`.

**Dry run** on `module.env["prod.sg"].module.db.aws_db_instance.this`:

| step | name | key |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | module | None |
| 1 | env | "prod.sg" |
| 2 | module | None |
| 3 | db | None |
| 4 | aws_db_instance | None |
| 5 | this | None |

Modules `[["env", "prod.sg"], ["db", None]]`, type `aws_db_instance`, name `this`.
guide.complexity: Time O(L) for an address of length L: each character is examined a constant number of times. Space O(L).
guide.pitfalls: Splitting on every dot (first wrong solution) breaks keys such as `"www.example.com"`. Leaving a numeric key as a string, or forgetting data sources (second wrong solution). Treating an empty quoted key as 'no key': `[""]` is the empty string, not `None`. Looking for `]` to end a quoted key, which fails when the key contains a bracket.
guide.follow_up: Write the inverse, `formatAddress(parsed)`, and check that formatting then parsing returns the original dict for every test.

tf-plan-summary.title: Summarise a plan
tf-plan-summary.description:
Terraform ends every plan with a one-line summary. Write `planSummary(actions)` that produces it.

`actions` is a list of strings, one per resource, each one of:
`"create"`, `"update"`, `"replace"`, `"delete"`, `"no-op"`.

Counting rules:

- `create` counts once under **add**.
- `update` counts once under **change**.
- `delete` counts once under **destroy**.
- `replace` counts once under **add** *and* once under **destroy** (the old object is destroyed and a new one created).
- `no-op` counts nowhere.

Return exactly `"Plan: A to add, C to change, D to destroy."`.
If all three numbers are zero (including an empty list), return
`"No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration."`.

**Example 1:** `["create", "update", "no-op"]` → `"Plan: 1 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy."`

**Example 2:** `["replace"]` → `"Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy."`

guide.prereqs: Reading a plan: the lesson *How Terraform works, and how it compares with the alternatives*. Python loops and f-strings.
guide.intuition: The summary is three counters. The only subtlety is that a replacement is two real operations, a destroy and a create, so it feeds two counters and never the *change* counter.
hints: Keep three integers and walk the list once.
Which counters does `replace` touch? Think about what physically happens to the old and the new object.
After the loop, check whether all three counters are zero before building the `Plan:` string.
guide.brute_force: Call `list.count` once per action name: five passes over the list. Still O(n), but the single loop is clearer about `replace` contributing twice.
guide.approach:
1. Start `add = change = destroy = 0`.
2. For each action: `create` → add; `update` → change; `delete` → destroy; `replace` → add **and** destroy; `no-op` → nothing.
3. If all are zero, return the "No changes" sentence; otherwise format the summary.

**Dry run** on `["delete", "replace", "create", "update", "no-op", "update"]`:

| action | add | change | destroy |
|---|---|---|---|
| delete | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| replace | 1 | 0 | 2 |
| create | 2 | 0 | 2 |
| update | 2 | 1 | 2 |
| no-op | 2 | 1 | 2 |
| update | 2 | 2 | 2 |

Result: `Plan: 2 to add, 2 to change, 2 to destroy.`
guide.complexity: Time O(n) for n actions, one pass. Space O(1): three counters.
guide.pitfalls: Counting `replace` as a change. Forgetting the destroy half of a replacement, which hides data loss. Printing `Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.` instead of the no-changes sentence. Missing the final full stop.
guide.follow_up: Real Terraform adds a fourth number, `N to import`, when import blocks are present. Extend the function to accept an `import` action.

tests.expected: Plan: 1 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy.
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.
No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.
No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.
Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.
Plan: 11 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
Plan: 2 to add, 1 to change, 2 to destroy.
Plan: 2 to add, 2 to change, 2 to destroy.
Plan: 0 to add, 3 to change, 0 to destroy.
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.
Plan: 40 to add, 0 to change, 40 to destroy.
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.

tf-compute-plan.title: Compute a plan from desired configuration and state
tf-compute-plan.description:
Build the heart of `terraform plan`. Write `computePlan(desired, state, force_new)`.

- `desired` maps a resource address to its attributes as written in the configuration, e.g.
  `{"aws_instance.web": {"ami": "ami-2", "size": "small"}}`.
- `state` has the same shape and holds what Terraform recorded last time.
- `force_new` maps a **resource type** to a list of attribute names that cannot be changed in place.
  The resource type is the part of the address before the first dot (`aws_instance` for `aws_instance.web`).
  A type missing from `force_new` has no such attributes.

For every address that appears in `desired` or `state`, decide one action:

| Situation | Action |
|---|---|
| In `desired` only | `"create"` |
| In `state` only | `"delete"` |
| In both, all attributes equal | `"no-op"` |
| In both, at least one changed attribute is force-new for its type | `"replace"` |
| In both, something changed but nothing force-new | `"update"` |

An attribute counts as **changed** when its value differs between the two sides, or when it is present on
one side and absent on the other.

Return a list of `[address, action]` pairs sorted by address.

**Example:** desired `{"aws_instance.web": {"ami": "ami-2"}}`, state `{"aws_instance.web": {"ami": "ami-1"}, "aws_s3_bucket.logs": {"name": "l"}}`,
force_new `{"aws_instance": ["ami"]}` → `[["aws_instance.web", "replace"], ["aws_s3_bucket.logs", "delete"]]`

guide.prereqs: The plan table in *How Terraform works, and how it compares with the alternatives*. Python dicts and sets.
guide.intuition: A plan is a diff between two dictionaries, taken twice: first over the set of addresses (who exists on which side), then, for addresses on both sides, over the set of attribute names. One extra question decides between update and replace: did any changed attribute belong to the type's force-new list?
hints: Take the union of the two key sets and sort it; handle 'only in desired' and 'only in state' first.
For an address on both sides, collect the attribute names that differ. Remember an attribute can be missing on either side.
Intersect the changed names with `force_new[type]`. Non-empty means replace.
guide.brute_force: Compare every address in `desired` against every address in `state` with nested loops to find matches: O(n·m). Dictionary lookups make the match O(1) per address.
guide.approach:
1. `addresses = sorted(set(desired) | set(state))`.
2. Not in state → `create`. Not in desired → `delete`.
3. Otherwise compute `changed`: for each key in the union of both attribute dicts, compare the two values, using a unique sentinel for "absent" so that a missing key differs even from `None`.
4. Empty `changed` → `no-op`. If `changed` intersects the type's force-new list → `replace`, else `update`.

**Dry run** with force_new `{"aws_instance": ["ami"]}`:

- `aws_instance.web`: desired `{ami: b, size: large}`, state `{ami: a, size: small}` → changed `{ami, size}`; `ami` is force-new → **replace**. One force-new attribute is enough, even if others could have been updated in place.
- `aws_s3_bucket.logs`: only in state → **delete**.
guide.complexity: Time O(R log R + A) where R is the number of addresses and A the total number of attributes; the sort dominates. Space O(R) for the result.
guide.pitfalls: Iterating only over the desired attributes, which misses an attribute that was removed from the configuration. Using `dict.get(k)` on both sides, which treats a missing key and an explicit `None` as equal. Looking up `force_new` by full address instead of by type. Forgetting to sort.
guide.follow_up: Real providers also have computed attributes that are unknown until apply. Extend the model with an `UNKNOWN` marker that never counts as a change.

tf-plan-review.title: Flag destructive actions in a plan
tf-plan-review.description:
A reviewer's first job is to find every line of a plan that destroys something. Write
`reviewPlan(changes, protected_types)`.

`changes` is a list of dicts shaped like entries of Terraform's plan JSON:

```
{"address": "aws_db_instance.orders", "type": "aws_db_instance", "actions": ["delete", "create"]}
```

`actions` is one of `["create"]`, `["update"]`, `["delete"]`, `["no-op"]`, `["delete", "create"]`
(replace, destroy first) or `["create", "delete"]` (replace, create first).

`protected_types` is a list of resource types that hold data (databases, buckets, disks).

Produce one flag for every change whose actions include `"delete"`:

- `"REPLACE <address>"` if the actions also include `"create"`, otherwise `"DESTROY <address>"`;
- append `" [PROTECTED]"` if the change's `type` is in `protected_types`.

Return the flags with all protected ones first, and within each group sorted by address.

**Example:** the change above with `protected_types = ["aws_db_instance"]` → `["REPLACE aws_db_instance.orders [PROTECTED]"]`
tf-plan-review.solution:
def reviewPlan(changes, protected_types):
    protected = set(protected_types)
    rows = []
    for c in changes:
        actions = c["actions"]
        if "delete" not in actions:
            continue
        kind = "REPLACE" if "create" in actions else "DESTROY"
        is_protected = c["type"] in protected
        text = f"{kind} {c['address']}" + (" [PROTECTED]" if is_protected else "")
        rows.append((0 if is_protected else 1, c["address"], text))
    rows.sort()
    return [r[2] for r in rows]

guide.prereqs: Plan JSON and `resource_changes` from *Testing, part 1: manual tests, static analysis, policy and plan testing*.
guide.intuition: Every destructive change has `delete` somewhere in its action list. A replacement is a delete that happens to come with a create, and it destroys data exactly like a plain delete does.
hints: Filter first: keep only the changes whose actions contain `delete`.
Both `["delete", "create"]` and `["create", "delete"]` are replacements.
Sort by a pair: (not protected, address). Sorting the finished strings would order by the words DESTROY and REPLACE instead.
guide.brute_force: Build one list for protected flags and another for the others, sort each by address, and concatenate. Equivalent in cost; a tuple sort key does it in one pass.
guide.approach:
For each change with `delete` in its actions, compute `kind` (REPLACE when `create` is also present), whether the type is protected, and the text. Collect `(0 or 1, address, text)` and sort.

**Dry run:** changes `b.x` delete, `a.x` delete, `c.x` replace, with `c` protected.

| tuple | text |
|---|---|
| (1, "b.x") | DESTROY b.x |
| (1, "a.x") | DESTROY a.x |
| (0, "c.x") | REPLACE c.x [PROTECTED] |

Sorted: `REPLACE c.x [PROTECTED]`, `DESTROY a.x`, `DESTROY b.x`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n log n) for the sort over n changes; space O(n).
guide.pitfalls: Testing `actions == ["delete"]`, which lets replacements through unflagged: the most dangerous omission. Sorting the output strings, which groups by kind instead of by protection. Treating `update` on a protected type as destructive.
guide.follow_up: Add a threshold: return an extra line `TOO MANY DELETIONS` when more than k resources are destroyed in one plan.

tf-policy-check.title: Check a plan against policy rules
tf-policy-check.description:
Policy-as-code tools read the plan JSON and fail the pipeline when a rule is broken. Write
`checkPolicy(changes, rules)`.

Each change is a dict: `{"address", "type", "actions", "after"}`. `after` is a dict of the resource's
planned attributes, or `None` for a pure delete.

**Which changes are checked.** Only changes whose `actions` include `"create"` or `"update"`.
Changes that are exactly `["no-op"]` or exactly `["delete"]` are skipped: existing, untouched
resources are not this plan's responsibility.

`rules` is a dict with three keys:

1. `"required_tags"`: a list of tag names. For every checked change and every listed tag (in the listed
   order), if `after.get("tags", {})` lacks the tag or maps it to an empty string, report
   `"<address>: missing tag <tag>"`.
2. `"allowed_instance_types"`: a list. For a checked change of type `aws_instance` whose
   `after["instance_type"]` is present and not in the list, report
   `"<address>: instance type <value> not allowed"`. An empty list means the rule is off.
3. `"forbid_public_buckets"`: a bool. When true, for a checked change of type `aws_s3_bucket` whose
   `after.get("acl")` is `"public-read"` or `"public-read-write"`, report `"<address>: public bucket"`.

Return all violation strings sorted alphabetically.

**Example:** creating `aws_instance.batch` with `{"instance_type": "m5.24xlarge", "tags": {}}` under rules
`{"required_tags": ["Team"], "allowed_instance_types": ["t3.micro"], "forbid_public_buckets": true}` →
`["aws_instance.batch: instance type m5.24xlarge not allowed", "aws_instance.batch: missing tag Team"]`

guide.prereqs: Policy as code and the plan JSON in *Testing, part 1: manual tests, static analysis, policy and plan testing*.
guide.intuition: A policy engine is a loop over `resource_changes` that applies each rule to the resources the plan is about to create or modify, and collects messages. Deciding *which resources are in scope* matters as much as the rules themselves.
hints: Start with the scope filter: is `create` or `update` in the actions?
`after` may be `None`, and `tags` may be missing or `None`. Normalise both to empty dicts before checking.
An empty tag value is as bad as a missing tag; an empty allowed list switches the instance rule off; two ACL values count as public.
guide.brute_force: Run three separate passes over the changes, one per rule, and concatenate. Same O(n) cost; one pass keeps the scope filter in a single place.
guide.approach:
For each change:

1. Skip unless `create` or `update` is among the actions. Replacements pass, because they contain `create`.
2. `after = change["after"] or {}` and `tags = after.get("tags") or {}`.
3. For each required tag: `if not tags.get(tag)` → message. This catches both absent and empty.
4. Instance rule: only type `aws_instance`, only when the allowed list is non-empty and the attribute exists.
5. Bucket rule: only when the flag is true.

Sort the collected messages.

**Dry run:** a `no-op` instance with a huge type and no tags, plus a deleted bucket → both skipped → `[]`. That is the correct result: the plan does not touch them.
guide.complexity: Time O(n·t + v log v) for n changes, t required tags and v violations; space O(v).
guide.pitfalls: Checking `no-op` resources, which makes every unrelated pull request fail on old debt. Crashing on `after = None`. Using `tag not in tags`, which accepts an empty value. Applying the instance rule when the allowed list is empty. Forgetting `public-read-write`.
guide.follow_up: Add a rule that forbids deleting resources of protected types, and a way to exempt a specific address with a recorded reason.

expected: aws_instance.batch: instance type m5.24xlarge not allowed
aws_instance.a: instance type c5.large not allowed
aws_instance.z: instance type c5.large not allowed
aws_instance.n03: instance type m5.large not allowed
aws_instance.n09: instance type m5.large not allowed
aws_instance.n15: instance type m5.large not allowed

tf-cost-estimate.title: Estimate the cost change of a plan
tf-cost-estimate.description:
Cost tools read a plan and a price list and report how the monthly bill will move. Write
`costDelta(changes, prices)`.

Each change is a dict `{"type", "actions", "before", "after"}` where `before` and `after` are the
resource's **size** (a string such as `"t3.micro"`) or `None`.

`prices` maps `"<type>:<size>"` to a whole-number monthly price, for example
`{"aws_instance:t3.micro": 8}`. A type with no meaningful size uses an empty size: `"aws_lb:"`.
When `before` or `after` is `None` the size is the empty string for lookup purposes.
A key missing from `prices` costs `0`.

Rules per change:

- `["create"]`: the plan **adds** the price of `after`.
- `["delete"]`: the plan **removes** the price of `before`.
- `["update"]`, and both replacement orders: it removes the price of `before` and adds the price of `after`.
- `["no-op"]`: nothing.

Return `[added, removed, net]` where `added` and `removed` are the two totals and `net = added - removed`.

**Example:** one instance updated from `t3.micro` (8) to `t3.large` (60) and one load balancer created (18)
→ `[78, 8, 70]`

guide.prereqs: Plan actions, and the review summary in *Terraform as a team, part 2: golden rules and a CI/CD pipeline*.
guide.intuition: Think of each change as moving money between two piles: what the plan starts paying for and what it stops paying for. An in-place resize does both, exactly like a replacement, even though no resource is destroyed.
hints: Write a small `price(type, size)` helper that builds the key and defaults to 0.
Decide two booleans per change: does it add the `after` price? does it remove the `before` price?
`update` is true for both. `create` only adds, `delete` only removes.
guide.brute_force: There is nothing slower that is natural here; the straightforward loop is already linear. The risk is in the case analysis, not the speed.
guide.approach:
For each change that is not `no-op`:

- `adds = "create" in actions or "update" in actions`
- `removes = "delete" in actions or "update" in actions`

Add `price(type, after)` when `adds`, add `price(type, before)` to the removed total when `removes`.

**Dry run** with prices micro = 8, large = 60, load balancer = 18:

| change | added | removed |
|---|---|---|
| instance update micro → large | 60 | 8 |
| load balancer create (size None → key `aws_lb:`) | 78 | 8 |

Result `[78, 8, 70]`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), one dictionary lookup or two per change. Space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: Ignoring `update`, which hides the most common source of cost growth: resizing. Charging the `before` price on a pure create with a `None` size when a sizeless price such as `aws_lb:` exists. Looking up a size under the wrong resource type. Treating an unknown price as an error instead of zero.
guide.follow_up: Return the three most expensive individual changes so a reviewer sees where the money goes.

tf-blast-radius.title: Rank changes by blast radius
tf-blast-radius.description:
The **blast radius** of a change is everything that could be affected if it goes wrong. For one resource,
define it as the resource itself plus every resource that depends on it, directly or through a chain.

Write `blastRadius(depends_on, changed)`.

- `depends_on` maps each resource address to the list of addresses it depends on. Every resource in the
  system appears as a key (possibly with an empty list). Dependencies on addresses that are not keys are ignored.
  The graph has no cycles.
- `changed` is a list of addresses being modified by a plan (all are keys of `depends_on`, no duplicates).

For each changed address compute the size of its blast radius. Return a list of `[address, size]` pairs
ordered by size descending, ties broken by address ascending.

**Example:** `{"vpc": [], "subnet": ["vpc"], "db": ["subnet"], "app": ["subnet", "db"], "dns": []}` with
`changed = ["db", "vpc", "dns"]` → `[["vpc", 4], ["db", 2], ["dns", 1]]`.
Changing the VPC can affect the subnet, the database and the app as well as itself.

guide.prereqs: The dependency graph in *Variables, outputs, references and a configurable web server*; blast radius in *Isolating state: workspaces, file layout and reading another state*. Graph traversal (depth-first or breadth-first search).
guide.intuition: `depends_on` points from a resource to what it needs. Damage flows the other way: from a resource to whatever needs *it*. Reverse the arrows once, then the blast radius of a node is the number of nodes reachable from it.
hints: Build a reversed adjacency list: for each `a` depending on `b`, record that `a` is a dependent of `b`.
From each changed address, traverse the reversed graph with a `seen` set. The answer is the size of the set.
A diamond (two paths to the same node) must be counted once. That is what the `seen` set guarantees.
guide.brute_force: For each changed address, scan the whole `depends_on` dict to find direct dependents, then scan again for each of those, and so on: O(V·E) per start. Precomputing the reversed graph makes each traversal O(V + E).
guide.approach:
1. `dependents[b]` = list of addresses that list `b` among their dependencies (ignoring unknown addresses).
2. For each changed address run an iterative depth-first search over `dependents`, keeping a `seen` set that starts with the address itself.
3. Sort by `(-size, address)`.

**Dry run** on the example. Reversed graph: `vpc → [subnet]`, `subnet → [db, app]`, `db → [app]`.

- `vpc`: seen grows `{vpc}` → `{vpc, subnet}` → `{vpc, subnet, db, app}`; `app` is reached twice but counted once → 4.
- `db`: `{db, app}` → 2.
- `dns`: nothing depends on it → 1.

Sorted: `[["vpc", 4], ["db", 2], ["dns", 1]]`.
guide.complexity: Time O(V + E) to reverse, then O(V + E) per changed address: O(k·(V + E)) for k changes, plus O(k log k) to sort. Space O(V + E).
guide.pitfalls: Counting only direct dependents. Recursively summing counts without a visited set, which double-counts diamonds (the second wrong solution). Traversing in the dependency direction, which measures what a resource needs instead of what it can break. Deep recursion on a long chain.
guide.follow_up: Weight each resource (a database counts 10, a tag change 1) and rank by total weight. This is how some review tools decide which pull requests need a second approver.

tf-workspace-key.title: Map workspaces to state objects in an S3 backend
tf-workspace-key.description:
With an S3 backend, one configuration can keep several separate state files, one per **workspace**. Knowing
exactly where each one is stored matters when you need to inspect, back up or restore state. Write
`statePaths(backend, workspaces)`.

`backend` is a dict holding the backend settings:

- `"bucket"`: the bucket name;
- `"key"`: the path of the state object inside the bucket, as configured;
- `"workspace_key_prefix"`: optional, defaults to `"env:"`;
- `"use_lockfile"`: optional bool, defaults to false. When true, Terraform locks by writing a lock object
  beside the state, named like the state object with `.tflock` added.

Rules for the object key:

- workspace `default` → the configured `key` unchanged;
- any other workspace → `<workspace_key_prefix>/<workspace>/<key>`.

Return a dict from each workspace name in `workspaces` to `[state_url, lock_url]`, where
`state_url` is `s3://<bucket>/<object key>` and `lock_url` is the state URL plus `.tflock` when
`use_lockfile` is true, otherwise `None`.

**Example:** backend `{"bucket": "acme-tfstate", "key": "app/terraform.tfstate", "use_lockfile": True}` and
workspaces `["default", "stage"]` →

```
{"default": ["s3://acme-tfstate/app/terraform.tfstate", "s3://acme-tfstate/app/terraform.tfstate.tflock"],
 "stage":   ["s3://acme-tfstate/env:/stage/app/terraform.tfstate", "s3://acme-tfstate/env:/stage/app/terraform.tfstate.tflock"]}
```

guide.prereqs: Backends and locking in *Terraform state, remote backends and locking*; workspaces in *Isolating state: workspaces, file layout and reading another state*. String building and `dict.get` with a default.
guide.intuition: A bucket is a filing cabinet and the `key` is the label on one folder. The `default` workspace uses that folder directly. Every other workspace gets the same label filed one level deeper, inside a drawer named after the prefix and then the workspace. The lock, when S3 locking is on, is a sticky note placed next to whichever folder is being edited.
hints: Read the two optional settings once, with their defaults, before the loop.
Only the exact name `default` is special. `Default` and `defaults` are ordinary workspaces.
Build the state URL first; the lock URL is that string plus a suffix, or `None`.
guide.brute_force: There is no meaningfully slower method; each workspace is one string concatenation. The work is in getting the three small rules right.
guide.approach:
1. `prefix = backend.get("workspace_key_prefix", "env:")`, `locking = backend.get("use_lockfile", False)`.
2. For each workspace: `default` → `key`; otherwise `prefix/workspace/key`.
3. `url = "s3://" + bucket + "/" + key`; lock is `url + ".tflock"` when locking.

**Dry run:** bucket `acme-tfstate`, key `live/prod/network/terraform.tfstate`, prefix `workspaces`, locking on.

| workspace | object key |
|---|---|
| default | live/prod/network/terraform.tfstate |
| blue | workspaces/blue/live/prod/network/terraform.tfstate |

Note where `blue` ended up: at the top of the bucket under `workspaces/`, not beside the default state under `live/prod/network/`. Anyone browsing the `live/prod` folder will not see it, which is one reason workspaces are a weak way to separate environments.
guide.complexity: Time O(w·L) for w workspaces and key length L; space the same for the result.
guide.pitfalls: Prefixing the `default` workspace too (first wrong solution). Hard-coding `env:` or always returning a lock path (second wrong solution): without `use_lockfile` there is no lock object. Appending the workspace after the key instead of before it (third wrong solution). Comparing workspace names case-insensitively.
guide.follow_up: Write the inverse used by `terraform workspace list`: given every object key in the bucket and the backend settings, return the workspace names that have a state object, always including `default`.

tf-state-lock.title: Simulate state locking
tf-state-lock.description:
A state lock lets one run at a time write to a state file. Write `lockLog(events)` that replays a sequence
